design_detail: Systematic review with random-effects meta-analyses: the journal summary of an AHRQ Comparative Effectiveness Review (No. 134, prepared by the RTI International–University of North Carolina Evidence-based Practice Center; ref. 9). Question: benefits and harms of medications for adults with alcohol use disorders in outpatient settings, covering the FDA-approved acamprosate, disulfiram and naltrexone (oral and injectable) and 23 off-label medications. Eligible: double-blind RCTs of at least 12 weeks against placebo or another medication; head-to-head prospective cohort studies for health outcomes; for harms, also non-randomized designs comparing two medications. 123 studies (122 RCTs and 1 cohort study, in 151 articles; 22,803 participants), 95 of them in meta-analyses. Risk differences (RDs) and weighted mean differences (WMDs) pooled separately for each medication and naltrexone formulation, with numbers needed to treat (NNT) or harm (NNH); trials at high or unclear risk of bias kept out of the main analyses; strength of evidence graded high, moderate, low or insufficient.
can_establish: The average added effect of each medication, beyond psychosocial co-intervention and placebo, on drinking in double-blind trials (12 to 52 weeks; for the main oral naltrexone pools 12 to 24 weeks, mostly 12) of adults with alcohol dependence treated as outpatients (mostly after detoxification), as published or obtained up to March 2014, and how often adverse events and withdrawal from trials because of adverse events occurred.
cannot_establish: Effects on mortality, injuries, crashes, quality of life or function (the trials were neither designed nor powered for them and the evidence was insufficient); effects in mild alcohol use disorder, without a goal of abstinence, without a psychosocial co-intervention or in primary care; durability beyond the trials' durations (52 weeks at most; 24 weeks in the main oral naltrexone pools); a ranking of medications (3 or 4 head-to-head trials and no indirect or network comparison); or whether acamprosate's pooled effect is real, since it was not significant in the trials at low risk of bias.

sample.recruitment: Searches of PubMed, the Cochrane Library, PsycINFO, CINAHL and EMBASE from 1 January 1970 to 11 October 2013 for the AHRQ report, updated to 1 March 2014 for this article, run by an Evidence-based Practice Center librarian and peer-reviewed by a second; ClinicalTrials.gov, the WHO International Clinical Trials Registry Platform and the FDA website for unpublished studies; manufacturers asked for unpublished studies and data through AHRQ's Scientific Resource Center; reference lists of reviews and trials; references suggested by reviewers (p. 1890; Figure 1, p. 1891). Trial participants were adults who met DSM-III or DSM-IV criteria for alcohol dependence in most trials, mostly enrolled after detoxification or a period of abstinence and usually receiving a psychosocial co-intervention; the largest trial, COMBINE, enrolled 1383 treatment-seeking patients (p. 1891). European acamprosate trials recruited mainly from inpatient settings or treatment programmes, US trials by advertisement and referral (p. 1896).
sample.inclusion_exclusion: Included: adults with an alcohol use disorder; an FDA-approved medication or any of 23 off-label medications given for at least 12 weeks in an outpatient setting; at least one outcome on consumption (return to any drinking, return to heavy drinking, drinking days, heavy drinking days, drinks per drinking day), health (motor vehicle crashes, injuries, quality of life, function, mortality) or adverse effects; double-blind RCTs against placebo or another medication; prospective cohorts comparing two medications if they reported a health outcome; for adverse effects also non-randomized or open-label trials, trial subgroup analyses, prospective cohorts and case-control studies comparing two medications (p. 1890). Excluded at full text (395 of 546 articles, Figure 1): publication type 23, population 38, intervention 22, comparator 64, outcome 64, setting 18, study design 111, duration under 12 weeks 46, not available in English 6, foreign-language publications of data also published in English 3. Of the 123 included studies, 28 were not pooled: 7 were the only study of a medication, 1 was not an RCT and 20 reported insufficient data (Figure 1, p. 1891).
sample.demographics: Sample sizes 21 to 1383; treatment 12 to 52 weeks; mean age usually in the 40s (p. 1891). The distribution of sex, race or ethnicity, smoking and coexisting conditions is not given in the article (study characteristics are in eTable 4, not read); the authors found no evidence on whether benefit differs by any of these (p. 1896). Placebo-controlled acamprosate trials: 16 of 22 in Europe, 4 in the US; naltrexone: 27 of 44 in the US, 8 in Europe (p. 1896).
sample.attrition: Not applicable at review level. Attrition, intention-to-treat analysis and the handling of missing data were risk-of-bias criteria (p. 1890), but the article does not say how participants lost to follow-up were counted in the binary return-to-drinking outcomes, which the forest plots give as events and non-events per arm (Figures 2 and 3).
sample.selection_effects: Efficacy-trial populations: adults with alcohol dependence (moderate to severe disorder in DSM-5 terms, in the authors' reading), mostly abstinent before starting medication and receiving psychosocial co-interventions; applicability to mild disorder, to people without a goal of abstinence and to primary care is uncertain, with only 2 eligible primary-care trials (pp. 1896–1897). Recruitment route differed by region and medication (European acamprosate trials from inpatient settings or treatment programmes; US trials by advertisement and referral), which the authors offer as one explanation of acamprosate's weaker results in US trials (pp. 1896–1897). Pools mix special populations named in the reference list, for example co-occurring depression (ref. 58), comorbid psychiatric disorders (ref. 69), comorbid cocaine dependence (ref. 78), bipolar disorder (ref. 43), older patients (ref. 68) and rural Alaska Native and non-Native communities (ref. 36). Six identified studies not available in English and 46 full-text articles with treatment shorter than 12 weeks were excluded (Figure 1).

exposure.measurement: The exposure is double-blind randomized assignment to a medication or to placebo in each trial, as the trials gave it. Medications were analysed one by one and never pooled by class (nalmefene and naltrexone, both opioid receptor antagonists, were kept apart), and naltrexone by formulation: oral 50 mg/day, oral 100 mg/day, injectable (pp. 1890–1891; Table 1). Adherence is not analysed at review level; incomplete reporting of fidelity and adherence was a common reason for a medium risk-of-bias rating (p. 1897).
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: Treatment lasted 12 to 52 weeks in the trials (p. 1891); oral medications and an injectable naltrexone formulation. The article gives doses only as the labels of the review's naltrexone analysis groups; doses of acamprosate and of the off-label medications are not given (eTable 4, not read). Recorded here only as study conditions.
exposure.polysubstance: Not handled at review level. Trials enrolling people with a dual diagnosis (for example alcohol dependence with depression) were pooled with the rest; sensitivity analyses stratified by whether trials enrolled a dual-diagnosis population did not change the acamprosate or naltrexone effect sizes significantly (data only in the full report; p. 1897). Use of other drugs within trials is not reported in the article; the authors found no evidence on whether benefit differs between people who smoke and people who do not (p. 1896).
exposure.abstinence_at_testing: Not applicable as a testing condition. Most trials required detoxification or at least 3 days' abstinence before medication began (p. 1891); a few enrolled people not yet abstinent and reported reduced heavy drinking with naltrexone (refs 44 and 96) or acamprosate (ref. 45) (p. 1896).

comparison.controls: Placebo given with the same psychosocial co-intervention as the medication arm, so the pooled effects are the added benefit of medication beyond co-intervention and placebo (p. 1891); in head-to-head trials, another medication (acamprosate vs naltrexone 4 trials; disulfiram vs naltrexone 1; naltrexone vs off-label medications 4). In multi-arm trials with one placebo group (COMBINE; Kiefer et al. 2003; Morley et al. 2006; Mann et al. 2013), that placebo group appears in separate pools, never twice in the same pool (editors' check of Figures 2 and 3).
comparison.matching: Randomization within trials; not applicable at review level.
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: Not an issue for the randomized within-trial contrasts. Between trials, disorder severity, recruitment route, country, abstinence before randomization and the kind of co-intervention varied and were not measured in a common way; the authors offer them as possible explanations of the acamprosate difference between US and European trials, without participant-level data to test them (pp. 1896–1897).

outcomes.instruments: Consumption: return to any drinking and return to heavy drinking (binary; the trials' own definitions, not stated in the article); percentage of drinking days; percentage of heavy drinking days (for nalmefene also heavy drinking days per month); drinks per drinking day. Health: accidents or injuries, quality of life or function (for example the SF-12 in COMBINE), mortality. Harms: withdrawal from trials due to adverse events and specific adverse events. How drinking was measured in the trials (self-report method, any biological check) is not described in the article. Strength of evidence was graded by two reviewers on risk of bias, consistency, directness and precision, following AHRQ guidance (ref. 18; p. 1890).
outcomes.validity_norms: Trial risk of bias was rated low, medium, high or unclear on predefined AHRQ criteria (randomization, allocation concealment, baseline similarity, blinding, attrition, validity and reliability of measures, intention-to-treat analysis, handling of missing data, fidelity) by two independent reviewers (p. 1890). Only 8 of 123 studies were rated low (4 of 27 acamprosate, 4 of 53 naltrexone); most were medium, chiefly for incomplete reporting of sequence generation, allocation concealment, fidelity, adherence or outcome-assessor masking (p. 1897).
outcomes.operationalization: A heavy drinking day was 4 or more drinks for women and 5 or more for men; no gram definition of a drink is given (p. 1890). A medication was judged to have an effect when the 95% CI of the pooled result did not cross 0; NNTs and NNHs were calculated only for significant pooled RDs (p. 1890). Negative effect sizes favour the medication over placebo (in Table 2, acamprosate over naltrexone). RDs are absolute differences in the proportion of participants (an RD of −0.09 is 9 percentage points) and WMDs are in the outcome's units, percentage points of days or drinks (Table 1 footnote b, p. 1892).
outcomes.multiplicity_correction: None. 19 counts the pooled estimates (2 or more studies) in Table 1 (16: FDA-approved medications against placebo) and Table 2 (3: acamprosate against naltrexone). The article also reports 6 pooled estimates for off-label medications, 2 pooled NNHs for withdrawal due to adverse events and 14 for specific adverse events, and refers to more in eTables 5 to 7 and to post hoc risk-of-bias subgroup analyses in eFigures 3 to 10 (not read). The strength-of-evidence grading, not a statistical correction, is the review's safeguard against chance findings.
outcomes.assessor_blinding: Eligible trials were double-blind; outcome-assessor masking was a risk-of-bias criterion and was often incompletely reported (p. 1897). At review level, screening, risk-of-bias rating and strength-of-evidence grading were done by two reviewers with consensus, and all extractions were checked by at least two investigators (p. 1890).

analysis.effect_sizes: Random-effects meta-analyses of RCTs (Stata metan), RDs for binary and WMDs for continuous outcomes with 95% CIs and I-squared; NNT or NNH from significant pooled RDs; no tau-squared or prediction intervals. Against placebo (Table 1; trials at low or medium risk of bias): acamprosate, return to any drinking RD −0.09 (−0.14 to −0.04), 16 trials, n=4847, I2=80.8%, NNT 12 (8 to 26), moderate strength of evidence; return to heavy drinking −0.01 (−0.04 to 0.03), 7 trials, n=2496, I2=0%, moderate; percentage of drinking days WMD −8.8 (−12.8 to −4.8), 13 trials, n=4485, moderate. Oral naltrexone 50 mg/day: return to any drinking −0.05 (−0.10 to −0.002), 16 trials, n=2347, I2=46.4%, NNT 20 (11 to 500), moderate; return to heavy drinking −0.09 (−0.13 to −0.04), 19 trials, n=2875, I2=43.7%, NNT 12 (8 to 26), moderate; percentage of drinking days −5.4 (−7.5 to −3.2), 15 trials, n=1992, moderate; percentage of heavy drinking days −4.1 (−7.6 to −0.61), 6 trials, n=521, moderate; drinks per drinking day −0.49 (−0.92 to −0.06), 9 trials, n=1018, low. Oral naltrexone 100 mg/day: return to any drinking −0.03 (−0.08 to 0.02), 3 trials, n=946; return to heavy drinking −0.05 (−0.11 to 0.01), 2 trials, n=858; percentage of drinking days −0.9 (−4.2 to 2.5), 2 trials, n=858; percentage of heavy drinking days −3.1 (−5.8 to −0.3), 2 trials, n=423; all low. Injectable naltrexone: return to any drinking −0.04 (−0.10 to 0.03), 2 trials, n=939; return to heavy drinking −0.01 (−0.14 to 0.13), 2 trials, n=615, I2=72.2%; percentage of heavy drinking days −4.6 (−8.5 to −0.56), 2 trials, n=926; all low. Disulfiram: return to any drinking −0.04 (−0.11 to 0.03), 2 trials, n=492, low. Head-to-head, acamprosate vs naltrexone (Table 2; negative favours acamprosate): return to any drinking 0.02 (−0.03 to 0.08), 3 trials, n=800, moderate; return to heavy drinking 0.01 (−0.05 to 0.06), 4 trials, n=1141, moderate; percentage of drinking days −2.98 (−13.4 to 7.5), 2 trials, n=720, low. Off-label (pp. 1894–1895): topiramate, percentage of drinking days −6.5 (−12.0 to −1.0), 2 trials, n=541; percentage of heavy drinking days −9.0 (−15.3 to −2.7), 3 trials, n=691; drinks per drinking day −1.0 (−1.6 to −0.48), 3 trials, n=691; nalmefene, heavy drinking days per month −2.0 (−3.0 to −1.0), 2 trials, n=806; drinks per drinking day −1.02 (−1.77 to −0.28), 3 trials, n=608; valproic acid, return to heavy drinking −0.32 (−0.52 to −0.11), 2 trials (Figure 3). Harms: withdrawal due to adverse events NNH 48 (30 to 112) for naltrexone, 17 trials, n=2743, and 12 (7 to 50) for nalmefene, 5 trials, n=2054; not significant for acamprosate or topiramate (p. 1895).
analysis.covariates: None at review level: within-trial randomized contrasts, no meta-regression. Post hoc subgroup analyses by risk of bias (eFigures 3 to 10), subgroups by population (for example US vs non-US trials; results not given numerically in the article), sensitivity analyses adding trials at high or unclear risk of bias (eFigures 1 and 2) and stratification by dual diagnosis (full report) (pp. 1890–1891, 1893, 1897).
analysis.preregistration_detail: The Methods state that a standard protocol was developed and followed and that a technical report detailing methods and search strategies is available online (ref. 9, AHRQ Comparative Effectiveness Review No. 134, not read); no registration number or protocol publication is given in the article (p. 1890). The risk-of-bias subgroup analyses are labelled post hoc (p. 1890).
analysis.selective_reporting: The article prints pooled numbers mainly for the FDA-approved medications. The off-label results and their strength-of-evidence grades (eTable 5), the adverse-event tables (eTables 6 and 7), the sensitivity and risk-of-bias subgroup forest plots, the US vs non-US subgroup results, and the funnel plots and Begg–Mazumdar results are in the supplement or the full report, not in the article; results for baclofen, gabapentin, varenicline and most other off-label medications are not given at all. The abstract gives acamprosate's NNT for return to any drinking but not its null result for return to heavy drinking, nor the null pooled result in the trials at low risk of bias. One pooled estimate (injectable naltrexone, heavy drinking days) includes data obtained by personal communication (Table 1 footnote e). The review searched for unpublished studies and outcomes and reports no direct evidence of selective reporting (p. 1897).
analysis.power: Not formally addressed. Many pools have 2 or 3 trials (all oral 100 mg/day and injectable naltrexone estimates, disulfiram, nalmefene, topiramate, valproic acid), and the post hoc risk-of-bias subgroups were underpowered for most outcomes by the authors' account (p. 1893). Deaths were too few to inform mortality: 13 in 2677 participants in the acamprosate trials and 3 in 1738 in the naltrexone trials (editors' arithmetic from Table 1).

interpretation_gap.results_show: Against placebo, with psychosocial co-interventions in both arms, acamprosate was associated with 9 percentage points fewer participants returning to any drinking (16 trials, NNT 12) but no difference in return to heavy drinking (7 trials, RD −0.01), and its effect on any drinking was not significant in the 4 trials at low risk of bias (RD −0.02, −0.09 to 0.05), the two largest of which were US trials that found no benefit. Oral naltrexone (50 mg/day group) was associated with 9 points fewer participants returning to heavy drinking (19 trials, NNT 12) and 5 points fewer returning to any drinking, with an interval reaching −0.002 (NNT up to 500). Three or four head-to-head trials, dominated by COMBINE, found no significant difference between acamprosate and naltrexone. Injectable naltrexone and disulfiram did not significantly change return to drinking. Trial evidence on mortality, injuries, crashes and quality of life was insufficient. Withdrawal from trials because of adverse events was more frequent with naltrexone (NNH 48) and nalmefene (NNH 12).
interpretation_gap.claimed: The abstract and Conclusions say that both acamprosate and oral naltrexone "were associated with reduction in return to drinking", that direct comparisons found no significant difference between them, and that dosing frequency, adverse events and availability may guide the choice (abstract, p. 1889; Conclusions, p. 1897). Gaps: (1) for acamprosate the abstract omits the null result for return to heavy drinking and the null pooled result in the trials at low risk of bias, which the Limitations discuss openly, naming a pooled effect that represents bias among the possible explanations (p. 1897); (2) the absence of a significant difference in 3 or 4 head-to-head trials is treated as grounds for choosing on convenience, although the placebo-controlled pools differ for heavy drinking (naltrexone RD −0.09 against acamprosate −0.01, a contrast the review does not test) and the head-to-head pool combines COMBINE's naltrexone arm, classed as 100 mg/day, with 50 mg/day arms without saying so (reporting issue 5); (3) the abstract reports the injectable-naltrexone reduction in heavy drinking days without saying that it rests on 2 trials, partly on data from a personal communication, and was graded low strength (Table 1); (4) the Discussion argues that improved health outcomes "should occur" with treatment, by extrapolation from epidemiology, a modelling study and a cost analysis, although the review found insufficient trial evidence on every health outcome (p. 1896); (5) the moderate-evidence statements for nalmefene and topiramate rest on grades in a supplement table not printed in the article. Against this, the article says plainly that its effect sizes are added benefits beyond psychosocial co-interventions, that applicability to mild disorder and primary care is uncertain, and that evidence on health outcomes and on many harms is insufficient; its use of association language for randomized evidence is cautious rather than overstated.

timeline.event: COMBINE (Anton et al., 2006; the review's ref. 30), the largest included trial (n=1383): by the review's account it found better drinking outcomes with naltrexone, a combined behavioural intervention or both than with placebo, and no evidence of efficacy for acamprosate; it is one of the two low risk-of-bias US trials behind the null low-risk acamprosate subgroup.

Rösner et al. (2010), Cochrane reviews of opioid antagonists and of acamprosate for alcohol dependence (on the project's Tier A list, read by another first reader in this round): the same comparisons, so their trial sets must be compared with this review's before the reviews are cited as independent support.
This review, the journal summary of AHRQ Comparative Effectiveness Review No. 134 (ref. 9), published with an editorial in the same issue (p. 1861; not on file, not read).

Palpacuer et al. (2015), PLOS Medicine review of nalmefene, listed on the project's Tier B list as a critique of the ESENSE 1 trial (Mann et al., 2013), which is one of the two trials behind this review's nalmefene heavy-drinking-days estimate (refs 80 and 81).
McPheeters et al. (2023), JAMA, listed on the project's Tier A list as the update of this review (read by another first reader in this round).

replication.where_it_stands: The baseline systematic review of medicines for alcohol use disorder on the project's list, since updated by McPheeters et al. (2023), whose card should be read alongside this one. Its firmest results are oral naltrexone for return to heavy drinking and acamprosate for return to any drinking, each with an NNT of 12 and moderate strength of evidence; the acamprosate result rests on European trials at medium risk of bias and was not reproduced in the low-risk US trials. The head-to-head trials show no significant difference between the two, trial evidence on health outcomes is insufficient, and the off-label grades rest on a supplement not on file. Overlap with the Rösner et al. (2010) Cochrane reviews and with McPheeters et al. (2023) is expected and must be checked before these reviews are cited together. Letters in reply to this article were not searched (no browser in this round).

funding.funder: Agency for Healthcare Research and Quality (AHRQ), US Department of Health and Human Services, contract HHSA290201200008I_HHSA29032002T. AHRQ staff helped develop the scope of work and reviewed drafts, and AHRQ approval was required before submission; the authors state they alone were responsible for the content and the decision to submit, and that AHRQ staff took no part in conducting the review, data collection or management, analysis, interpretation or manuscript preparation (pp. 1897–1898).
funding.declared_conflicts: All authors completed the ICMJE disclosure form and none were reported (p. 1897).
funding.affiliations_note: Authors from the University of North Carolina at Chapel Hill (Department of Medicine; Cecil G. Sheps Center for Health Services Research; Gillings School of Global Public Health; Department of Psychiatry; Bowles Center for Alcohol Studies), RTI International, the North Carolina Translational and Clinical Sciences Institute and Duke University; the RTI International–University of North Carolina Evidence-based Practice Center prepared the AHRQ report (p. 1897; ref. 9). The last author, J. C. Garbutt, is first author of an included trial of injectable naltrexone (Garbutt et al., 2005; ref. 44), which carries 62% of the weight in the injectable-naltrexone return-to-any-drinking pool (Figure 2, p. 1893); the article describes no procedure for appraising the authors' own trials. Funding of the included trials, including any by manufacturers, is not reported in the article.

what_would_settle_it: A large, multi-country, double-blind trial at low risk of bias comparing acamprosate, oral naltrexone and placebo, recruiting both from treatment programmes and from the community and across the range of disorder severity, followed beyond a year, with pre-registered drinking outcomes checked against biomarkers and with health outcomes (injuries, hospital admissions, liver disease, deaths) as powered endpoints; an individual-participant-data meta-analysis of the existing trials could test now whether severity, recruitment route, abstinence before randomization or country explains why acamprosate's effect disappears in the low-risk US trials.

domains.domain: 1. PICO components in research question and inclusion criteria
domains.note: Adults with alcohol use disorders in outpatient settings; FDA-approved and 23 off-label medications given for at least 12 weeks; placebo or another medication; consumption, health and adverse-effect outcomes (Methods › Study Selection, p. 1890).

The Methods open by saying a standard protocol was developed and followed and that a technical report detailing methods and search strategies is online (ref. 9), but no registration, publication or citation of the protocol itself is given and its content and timing are not described; the risk-of-bias subgroup analyses are labelled post hoc (p. 1890). As on other project cards, a stated but unregistered, undescribed protocol is judged no. A lenient reading would give partial yes, since the question, search, eligibility criteria and risk-of-bias method are all described in the Methods; the AHRQ report (not read) may say more.

Eligible designs are listed by outcome (double-blind RCTs for efficacy; head-to-head prospective cohorts for health outcomes; for harms also non-randomized trials, trial subgroups, cohorts and case-control studies comparing two medications), but no reason is given for these choices; only the 12-week minimum is explained (Limitations, 1st paragraph, p. 1897).

Five databases from 1970 to March 2014 with the search peer-reviewed by a second librarian, ClinicalTrials.gov, the WHO registry platform and the FDA website, unpublished studies and data requested from manufacturers, reference lists, references suggested by reviewers, and a search ending about 2.5 months before publication (pp. 1889–1890; Figure 1): every criterion for yes is met except that 6 identified studies not available in English were excluded with no stated reason (Figure 1 and footnote a, which names them, with sizes of 45, 90, 71 and 127 where given). Applying item 4 as written (decision p-amstar2-item4), an unjustified language restriction is no. Under a lenient reading (few, small, named studies) every criterion for yes would be met. The search strategies themselves are in the technical report, not read.

Two investigators independently reviewed every title and abstract; studies marked by either underwent dual, independent full-text review, with conflicts resolved by consensus (Methods › Study Selection, 3rd paragraph, p. 1890).

Structured extraction forms; all extractions reviewed for completeness and accuracy by at least 2 investigators (Methods › Data Extraction and Risk of Bias Assessment, 1st paragraph, p. 1890). This meets the item's first criterion (at least two reviewers reached consensus on the extracted data); independent double extraction is not described.

domains.domain: 7. List of excluded studies with justification (critical)
domains.note: Figure 1 gives the number of full-text exclusions by reason (395 articles in 10 categories) and its footnote a names the 6 excluded for language, but no list of the excluded full-text studies with reasons is given in the article, and none of the supplement items it cites (eTables 1 to 7, eFigures 1 to 10, eDiscussion) is described as one. The AHRQ technical report (ref. 9, not read) may contain such a list; the article does not say so.

domains.domain: 8. Included studies described in adequate detail
domains.note: Provisional: the article describes the included studies only in aggregate (sizes 21 to 1383, 12 to 52 weeks, mean age in the 40s, alcohol dependence, mostly after detoxification, psychosocial co-interventions) and gives each pooled trial's duration and risk of bias in Figures 2 and 3; it places the characteristics of the included studies in eTable 4 of the Supplement (Results, 1st paragraph, p. 1891), which was not read.

domains.domain: 9. Satisfactory risk-of-bias assessment of included studies (critical)
domains.note: Predefined AHRQ criteria (randomization adequacy, allocation concealment, baseline similarity, blinding, attrition, validity and reliability of measures, intention-to-treat, handling of missing data, fidelity), rated low, medium, high or unclear by two independent reviewers (p. 1890). Selection of the reported result from among several outcomes or analyses, required for yes, is not among the listed criteria; selective reporting is addressed only at review level, by searching registries for unpublished outcomes (p. 1897). Ratings are shown for each pooled trial in Figures 2 and 3, with one inconsistency (reporting issue 1).

domains.domain: 10. Funding sources of included studies reported
domains.note: Not reported in the article; eTable 4 (not read) is described only as giving study characteristics.

Random-effects meta-analysis of RCTs only, by medication and by naltrexone formulation (classes deliberately not combined), with RDs and WMDs, 95% CIs and I-squared; trials at high or unclear risk of bias kept out of the main analyses and added in sensitivity analyses; qualitative synthesis where pooling was not appropriate (pp. 1890–1891). Weaknesses this item does not score: random-effects pools of only 2 or 3 trials; RDs pooled across trials of 12 to 52 weeks with very different placebo return rates (I-squared 80.8% for acamprosate and return to any drinking); no tau-squared or prediction intervals; and a head-to-head pool that mixes naltrexone doses without saying so (reporting issue 5).

domains.domain: 12. Impact of risk of bias on pooled results assessed
domains.note: Trials at high or unclear risk of bias were excluded from the main analyses and added in sensitivity analyses (similar results, eFigures 1 and 2), and post hoc subgroups restricted to low risk-of-bias trials were analysed (eFigures 3 to 10); the acamprosate subgroup result is reported in the text (pp. 1891, 1893–1894).

domains.domain: 13. Risk of bias accounted for in interpretation (critical)
domains.note: The strength-of-evidence grades incorporate risk of bias, and the Limitations discuss the null low-risk acamprosate subgroup, naming bias in the overall pooled effect as one possible explanation (p. 1897). The abstract and Conclusions do not carry this caveat (see the interpretation gap).

I-squared is given for every pool in Figures 2 and 3; sources were examined by subgroups (US vs non-US, risk of bias) and dual-diagnosis stratification, and recruitment, severity and country differences are discussed (pp. 1890, 1896–1897). The US vs non-US subgroup results are not reported numerically in the article.

Funnel plots and the Begg–Mazumdar test for pools of 10 or more studies, with no indication of bias, together with searches of registries, the FDA website and manufacturers for unpublished studies and outcomes; discussed in the Limitations (pp. 1890, 1897). The plots and test results are not shown in the article, and Begg's test has low power.

domains.domain: 16. Conflicts of interest and funding reported
domains.note: AHRQ funding with the contract number, the sponsor's role and the authors' ICMJE disclosures (none reported) are stated (pp. 1897–1898).

risk_of_bias.reasoning: Provisional: item 8 can be judged only from eTable 4 of the Supplement, which was not read; it is not a critical item and cannot change the rating. Three critical items are not met: 2 (a protocol is mentioned but not registered, cited or described), 4 (six studies not available in English were excluded without a stated reason) and 7 (no list of excluded studies with reasons), which gives critically low confidence under AMSTAR 2; critical item 9 is partly met and items 11, 13 and 15 are met. The rating is driven by documentation and by the project's strict readings of items 2 and 4 (decision p-amstar2-item4) more than by the conduct of the synthesis, which was careful: broad searching including registries, the FDA and manufacturers' unpublished data, duplicate screening and risk-of-bias rating, trials at high or unclear risk of bias kept out of the main analyses, heterogeneity and publication bias examined, and the evidence graded. Under lenient readings of items 2 and 4, and if the AHRQ report lists the excluded studies, the review would rate moderate confidence (non-critical weaknesses at items 3 and 10). It may be cited for the pooled consumption effects of oral naltrexone and acamprosate against placebo, with their strength-of-evidence grades, as the average added benefit beyond psychosocial co-interventions in trials of people with alcohol dependence, the acamprosate estimate always with the null result in the trials at low risk of bias; for the absence of a significant difference in the 3 or 4 head-to-head trials; and for the adverse-event NNHs. It may not be cited for health outcomes (insufficient evidence), for off-label medications beyond the figures printed in the article, or for mild disorder and primary care.

key_findings.finding: 123 studies (151 articles) were included: 122 double-blind RCTs and 1 prospective cohort, with 22,803 participants; 95 entered meta-analyses (28 were not pooled: 7 were the only study of a medication, 1 was not an RCT, 20 reported insufficient data). Most studied acamprosate (27 studies, n=7519), naltrexone (53 studies, n=9140) or both. Sample sizes ranged from 21 to 1383 and treatment from 12 to 52 weeks; mean age was usually in the 40s; participants met criteria for alcohol dependence in the vast majority of trials and were mostly enrolled after detoxification or at least 3 days' abstinence.
key_findings.note: The PDF prints the participant total with a thin space (22 803), which a text-matching check will not equate with 22,803.
key_findings.source_read: PDF PDFs/Alcohol/Jonas_2014_PharmacotherapyAUD_MA.pdf, pp. 1889 and 1891 (text; Figure 1 checked on the rendered page)

key_findings.finding: The review included 22 placebo-controlled trials of acamprosate, 4 of disulfiram and 44 of naltrexone; 4 trials compared acamprosate with naltrexone, 1 disulfiram with naltrexone and 4 naltrexone with off-label medications. Most trials included psychosocial co-interventions, so the effect sizes are the added benefit of medication beyond psychosocial treatment and placebo. The largest trial, COMBINE, randomized 1383 treatment-seeking patients to medical management with naltrexone, acamprosate, both or two placebos, with or without a combined behavioural intervention, or to the behavioural intervention alone without pills.

Consumption outcomes were return to any drinking, return to heavy drinking, percentage of drinking days, percentage of heavy drinking days (a heavy drinking day being 4 or more drinks for women and 5 or more for men; no gram definition of a drink is given) and drinks per drinking day. Pooled RDs are absolute: an RD of −0.09 means 9 percentage points fewer participants returned to drinking than with placebo; WMDs are in the outcome's units; negative values favour the medication. Only trials at low or medium risk of bias enter the main analyses and the participant numbers in Table 1.
key_findings.locator: Methods › Study Selection, 1st paragraph; Data Synthesis and Analysis, 1st paragraph (p. 1890); Table 1 footnotes a and b (p. 1892)
key_findings.source_read: PDF PDFs/Alcohol/Jonas_2014_PharmacotherapyAUD_MA.pdf, pp. 1890 and 1892 (text; Table 1 footnotes checked on the rendered page)

key_findings.finding: Acamprosate vs placebo: return to any drinking RD −0.09 (95% CI −0.14 to −0.04), 16 trials, n=4847, I2=80.8%, NNT 12 (8 to 26), moderate strength of evidence; return to heavy drinking RD −0.01 (−0.04 to 0.03), 7 trials, n=2496, I2=0%, no effect, moderate strength; percentage of drinking days WMD −8.8 (−12.8 to −4.8), 13 trials, n=4485, moderate; percentage of heavy drinking days and drinks per drinking day, 1 trial each, insufficient.
key_findings.locator: Results › Consumption Outcomes, 1st paragraph (p. 1891); Table 1, acamprosate rows (p. 1892); Figure 2 and Figure 3, acamprosate subtotals (pp. 1893–1894)
key_findings.note: Editors' arithmetic from the event counts in Figure 2: 83% of placebo participants (1893 of 2271) and 76% of acamprosate participants (1968 of 2576) returned to any drinking (crude totals, not the random-effects estimate), so most participants in both arms drank again during treatment. The crude difference (7.0 percentage points) is smaller than the pooled 9 because, with I2 80.8%, the random-effects weights give the two large US low-risk trials (COMBINE and Mason et al., 2006) 16% of the weight (7.73% and 8.34%) for 25% of the participants (1213 of 4847) and 28% of the events (editors' arithmetic from Figure 2).
key_findings.source_read: PDF PDFs/Alcohol/Jonas_2014_PharmacotherapyAUD_MA.pdf, pp. 1891–1894 (text; Table 1 and Figures 2 and 3 checked on the rendered pages)

key_findings.finding: In a post hoc subgroup analysis of acamprosate and return to any drinking, the effect shrank as risk of bias fell: RD −0.13 (−0.20 to −0.06; 3 trials, n=757) in trials at high or unclear risk, −0.11 (−0.16 to −0.06; 12 trials, n=3438) at medium risk, and −0.02 (−0.09 to 0.05; 4 trials, n=1409) at low risk, not significant. The 2 low-risk trials that contributed by far the most events (COMBINE and Mason et al., 2006) were both US trials recruiting by advertisement and referral and found no efficacy; most of the 15 trials at medium, high or unclear risk were European (1 US, 1 Brazil) and recruited from inpatient settings or treatment programmes. The authors list population differences, other heterogeneity, no true effect (the pooled effect representing bias), chance, or a combination as possible explanations.
key_findings.locator: Results › Consumption Outcomes, 2nd paragraph (p. 1893, continuing on p. 1894); Discussion › Limitations, 3rd paragraph (p. 1897)
key_findings.note: In Figure 2 the two large low-risk trials give RD −0.02 (−0.08 to 0.04) for COMBINE and 0.04 (0.00 to 0.08) for Mason et al. (2006), the latter's point estimate favouring placebo. The subgroup forest plot itself (eFigure 3) is in the Supplement, not read.
key_findings.source_read: PDF PDFs/Alcohol/Jonas_2014_PharmacotherapyAUD_MA.pdf, pp. 1893, 1894 and 1897 (text; Figure 2 checked on the rendered page)

key_findings.finding: Oral naltrexone 50 mg/day vs placebo: return to heavy drinking RD −0.09 (−0.13 to −0.04), 19 trials, n=2875, I2=43.7%, NNT 12 (8 to 26); return to any drinking RD −0.05 (−0.10 to −0.002), 16 trials, n=2347, I2=46.4%, NNT 20 (11 to 500); percentage of drinking days WMD −5.4 (−7.5 to −3.2), 15 trials, n=1992; percentage of heavy drinking days −4.1 (−7.6 to −0.61), 6 trials, n=521 (all moderate strength); drinks per drinking day −0.49 (−0.92 to −0.06), 9 trials, n=1018 (low strength).
key_findings.locator: Abstract › Results; Results › Consumption Outcomes, 1st paragraph (p. 1891); Table 1, naltrexone 50 mg oral rows (p. 1892); Figures 2 and 3, naltrexone 50 mg/d subtotals (pp. 1893–1894)
key_findings.note: Figure 2 prints the upper limit for return to any drinking as −0.00 (rounded); Table 1 and the abstract give −0.002, so the interval nearly reaches no effect, hence the NNT bound of 500. The 19 trials for return to heavy drinking lasted 12 weeks (17), 16 weeks (1) or 24 weeks (1), and the 16 for return to any drinking 12 to 24 weeks (Figures 2 and 3). Editors' arithmetic from the event counts (crude totals): return to heavy drinking 54% with placebo (698 of 1282) and 46% with naltrexone (728 of 1593); return to any drinking 68% (729 of 1066) and 63% (805 of 1281).
key_findings.source_read: PDF PDFs/Alcohol/Jonas_2014_PharmacotherapyAUD_MA.pdf, pp. 1889 and 1891–1894 (text; Table 1 and Figures 2 and 3 checked on the rendered pages)

key_findings.finding: Oral naltrexone 100 mg/day (COMBINE the largest trial): return to any drinking RD −0.03 (−0.08 to 0.02), 3 trials, n=946; return to heavy drinking −0.05 (−0.11 to 0.01), 2 trials, n=858; percentage of heavy drinking days WMD −3.1 (−5.8 to −0.3), 2 trials, n=423; all low strength. Injectable naltrexone: return to any drinking −0.04 (−0.10 to 0.03), 2 trials, n=939; return to heavy drinking −0.01 (−0.14 to 0.13), 2 trials, n=615, I2=72.2%; percentage of heavy drinking days −4.6 (−8.5 to −0.56), 2 trials, n=926; all low strength. Disulfiram: return to any drinking −0.04 (−0.11 to 0.03), 2 trials, n=492, low strength; no other consumption outcome could be pooled.
key_findings.locator: Abstract › Results; Table 1, naltrexone 100 mg oral, naltrexone injection and disulfiram rows, footnotes d and e (p. 1892); Figures 2 and 3 (pp. 1893–1894)
key_findings.note: The injectable-naltrexone heavy-drinking-days estimate contains data from a personal communication (B. Silverman, 14 November 2013; Table 1 footnote e), whose source is not described further.
key_findings.source_read: PDF PDFs/Alcohol/Jonas_2014_PharmacotherapyAUD_MA.pdf, pp. 1889 and 1892–1894 (text; Table 1 and Figures 2 and 3 checked on the rendered pages)

key_findings.finding: Disulfiram: well-controlled trials did not show reduced drinking; the largest (n=605) reported fewer drinking days only for the subset who drank and had complete assessments (162 of 605), not for the full randomized sample. No disulfiram trial evaluated supervised administration, which the authors say may underestimate its benefit in supervised treatment programmes.
key_findings.locator: Results › Consumption Outcomes, 1st paragraph (p. 1891); Table 1 footnote d (p. 1892); Discussion, 3rd paragraph (pp. 1895–1896)

key_findings.finding: Acamprosate vs naltrexone in head-to-head trials (COMBINE, Morley et al. 2006, Kiefer et al. 2003, Mann et al. 2013): return to any drinking RD 0.02 (−0.03 to 0.08), 3 trials, n=800; return to heavy drinking 0.01 (−0.05 to 0.06), 4 trials, n=1141 (both moderate strength); percentage of drinking days WMD −2.98 (−13.4 to 7.5), 2 trials, n=720 (low); negative values favour acamprosate. Withdrawal because of adverse events did not differ significantly; headache and vomiting were slightly more frequent with naltrexone.
key_findings.locator: Results › Consumption Outcomes, 3rd paragraph (p. 1894); Table 2 and Results › Adverse Effects, 1st paragraph (p. 1895)
key_findings.note: Editors' arithmetic: Table 2's participant totals equal the sums of these trials' acamprosate and naltrexone arms in Figures 2 and 3, so COMBINE supplies 612 of the 800 participants for return to any drinking (77%) and 612 of the 1141 for return to heavy drinking (54%), and its naltrexone arm is the one the review classes as 100 mg/day; the other three trials sit in the 50 mg/day pools.
key_findings.source_read: PDF PDFs/Alcohol/Jonas_2014_PharmacotherapyAUD_MA.pdf, pp. 1893–1895 (text; Table 2 and Figures 2 and 3 checked on the rendered pages)

key_findings.finding: Off-label medications: topiramate, percentage of drinking days WMD −6.5 (−12.0 to −1.0; 2 trials, n=541), percentage of heavy drinking days −9.0 (−15.3 to −2.7; 3 trials, n=691) and drinks per drinking day −1.0 (−1.6 to −0.48; 3 trials, n=691); nalmefene, heavy drinking days per month −2.0 (−3.0 to −1.0; 2 trials, n=806) and drinks per drinking day −1.02 (−1.77 to −0.28; 3 trials, n=608); valproic acid, return to heavy drinking RD −0.32 (−0.52 to −0.11) in 2 small trials (total n=88 in the text), one in people with bipolar disorder. The abstract and Conclusions call the nalmefene and topiramate evidence moderate.
key_findings.locator: Abstract › Results; Results › Consumption Outcomes, 4th paragraph (pp. 1894–1895); Figure 3, valproic acid (p. 1894); Conclusions (p. 1897)
key_findings.note: The strength-of-evidence grades for off-label medications are in eTable 5, not on file. By the reference list, one of the three topiramate trials (ref. 78) enrolled people with comorbid cocaine and alcohol dependence, and the nalmefene heavy-drinking-days estimate comes from the ESENSE 2 trial (ref. 80) and Mann et al. (2013; ref. 81).
key_findings.source_read: PDF PDFs/Alcohol/Jonas_2014_PharmacotherapyAUD_MA.pdf, pp. 1889, 1894, 1895 and 1897 (text; Figure 3 checked on the rendered page; reference list pp. 1898–1900)

key_findings.finding: One placebo-controlled trial each was included for aripiprazole, atomoxetine, desipramine, fluvoxamine, gabapentin, imipramine, olanzapine, ondansetron and paroxetine, and several for baclofen, buspirone, citalopram, fluoxetine, nalmefene, quetiapine, sertraline, topiramate, valproic acid and varenicline. For most off-label medications the evidence was insufficient or suggested no association with reduced drinking; the article prints pooled results only for topiramate, nalmefene and valproic acid, and the results for the others, including baclofen, gabapentin and varenicline, are only in eTable 5 (not read).
key_findings.locator: Results, 2nd paragraph (p. 1891); Results › Consumption Outcomes, 4th paragraph (p. 1894)

key_findings.finding: Trial evidence was insufficient for every health outcome. No trial of an FDA-approved medication reported accidents or injuries; quality of life or function was reported in 1 acamprosate trial (n=612, no significant difference) and 4 naltrexone trials (n=1513, conflicting: 2 found no difference, 1 injectable-naltrexone trial found greater improvement on the mental health summary score at 24 weeks, 8.2 vs 6.2, P=.04, and 1 trial found fewer participants with at least one alcohol-related consequence, 45% vs 76%, P=.02, 34 per group); mortality was 7 deaths with acamprosate vs 6 with placebo (8 trials, n=2677) and 1 with naltrexone vs 2 with placebo (6 trials, n=1738). The trials were not designed or powered for health outcomes; in COMBINE an improvement on the SF-12 physical health scale with naltrexone plus behavioural intervention did not reach a clinically meaningful threshold.
key_findings.locator: Table 1, accidents or injuries, QoL or function and mortality rows, footnote f (p. 1892); Results › Health Outcomes, 1st paragraph (p. 1895)
key_findings.source_read: PDF PDFs/Alcohol/Jonas_2014_PharmacotherapyAUD_MA.pdf, pp. 1892 and 1895 (text; Table 1 checked on the rendered page)

key_findings.finding: Withdrawal from trials because of adverse events was more frequent than with placebo for naltrexone (NNH 48, 30 to 112; 17 trials, n=2743) and nalmefene (NNH 12, 7 to 50; 5 trials, n=2054), not significantly for acamprosate or topiramate. Significant NNHs for specific adverse events: acamprosate, anxiety 7 (5 to 11; 2 trials, n=624), diarrhoea 11 (6 to 34; 12 trials, n=2978), vomiting 42 (24 to 143; 4 trials, n=1817); naltrexone, dizziness 16 (12 to 28; 13 trials, n=2675), nausea 9 (7 to 14; 24 trials, n=4655), vomiting 24 (17 to 44; 9 trials, n=2438); nalmefene, dizziness 7 (5 to 10; 4 trials, n=1944), headache 26 (15 to 143; 3 trials, n=1401), insomnia 10 (8 to 17; 5 trials, n=2049), nausea 7 (5 to 11; 5 trials, n=2049), vomiting 17 (11 to 48; 3 trials, n=1679); topiramate, cognitive dysfunction 12 (7 to 84; 2 trials, n=521), paresthesias 4 (3 to 7; 3 trials, n=691), taste abnormalities 7 (5 to 15; 2 trials, n=477). For many other adverse events the evidence was insufficient because of imprecision; most point estimates favoured placebo.
key_findings.source_read: PDF PDFs/Alcohol/Jonas_2014_PharmacotherapyAUD_MA.pdf, p. 1895 (text; the adverse-event tables, eTables 6 and 7, were not read)

key_findings.finding: Most placebo-controlled acamprosate trials were European (16 of 22; 4 in the US) and most naltrexone trials were from the US (27 of 44; 8 in Europe). The few US acamprosate trials did not find it efficacious; European acamprosate trials typically recruited from inpatient settings or treatment programmes and US trials through advertisements and referrals, which the authors suggest may have produced populations differing in severity and potential for benefit.

Applicability: most participants met DSM-III or DSM-IV criteria for alcohol dependence, likely moderate to severe disorder in DSM-5 terms, so applicability to mild disorder is uncertain; there was no evidence on whether benefit differs by age, sex, race or ethnicity, smoking or coexisting conditions; medications were not compared with psychosocial treatments, and benefit for people without a goal of abstinence was not assessed. Two trials were in primary care: acamprosate (n=100, recruited mainly by advertisement in 2 family medicine settings) showed no significant effect; nalmefene (15 Finnish sites, about half in primary care) showed no difference in percentage of drinking days but a lower percentage of heavy drinking days (18.1% vs 29.7%, P=.02) and fewer drinks per drinking day (WMD −1.0, −2.0 to −0.02).
key_findings.locator: Discussion › Applicability of Findings, 1st paragraph; Applicability to Primary Care Settings, 3rd paragraph (p. 1896); Limitations, 1st paragraph (p. 1897)

key_findings.finding: Only 8 of 123 studies were rated low risk of bias (4 of 27 acamprosate, 4 of 53 naltrexone); most were medium, chiefly for incomplete reporting of sequence generation, allocation concealment, fidelity, adherence or outcome-assessor masking. Adding the trials at high or unclear risk of bias gave results similar to the main analyses (eFigures 1 and 2), and stratifying by dual diagnosis did not change the effect sizes significantly (data only in the full report).
key_findings.locator: Results › Consumption Outcomes, 1st paragraph (end, p. 1891); Discussion › Limitations, 2nd and 3rd paragraphs (p. 1897)

key_findings.finding: The searches covered PubMed, the Cochrane Library, PsycINFO, CINAHL and EMBASE from 1 January 1970 to 11 October 2013 for the technical report, updated to 1 March 2014 for the article, plus ClinicalTrials.gov, the WHO registry platform, the FDA website and manufacturers' unpublished data. Figure 1: 6089 database records and 426 from other sources; 2586 duplicates removed; 3929 records screened; 546 full texts assessed; 395 excluded, 6 of them because they were not available in English. Funnel plots and the Begg–Mazumdar test, used where 10 or more studies were pooled, did not indicate publication bias; the plots and test results are not shown.
key_findings.locator: Methods › Data Sources and Searches, 1st and 2nd paragraphs; Data Synthesis and Analysis, 1st paragraph (p. 1890); Figure 1 and its footnote a (p. 1891)
key_findings.source_read: PDF PDFs/Alcohol/Jonas_2014_PharmacotherapyAUD_MA.pdf, pp. 1890 and 1891 (text; Figure 1 checked on the rendered page)

key_findings.finding: The Discussion argues that improved health outcomes should follow treatment, because epidemiological studies link heavy drinking to cancers, cirrhosis, pancreatitis, stroke, depression, suicide, injuries and violence; it cites a modelling study estimating that treatment coverage of 40% of people with alcohol dependence in the European Union would reduce alcohol-attributable mortality by up to 13% (ref. 92) and a COMBINE cost analysis in which several treatment combinations reduced costs of health care, arrests and motor vehicle accidents (ref. 93). These are cited findings, not results of this review.
key_findings.note: Second-hand figures: a claim on treatment and mortality would have to rest on the cited modelling study itself, not on this review.

reporting_issues.issue: Kiefer et al. (2003; ref. 39) is rated low risk of bias in both its acamprosate and its naltrexone rows of Figure 2 (return to any drinking), but in Figure 3 (return to heavy drinking) its acamprosate comparison is rated medium and its naltrexone comparison low, although the two comparisons share one placebo group.
reporting_issues.consequence: The Methods describe one risk-of-bias rating per study, so either ratings were made per outcome or comparison without saying so, or one label is wrong; the count of low-risk acamprosate studies (4 of 27) and the low-risk subgroup analyses depend on these labels and cannot be fully reconstructed from the article.

reporting_issues.issue: Table 1 gives 492 participants for disulfiram and return to any drinking (2 trials), while by editors' arithmetic the event counts for the same two trials in Figure 2 sum to 486 (Fuller et al. 1979: 43 and 42; Fuller et al. 1986: 202 and 199). Every other participant total in Table 1 that can be checked against Figures 2 and 3 matches.
reporting_issues.consequence: A small, unexplained difference (perhaps randomized versus analysed participants); the pooled estimate is unaffected, but the n should be quoted with this caveat.

reporting_issues.issue: The text gives a total n of 88 for the 2 valproic acid trials, while by editors' arithmetic their counts in Figure 3 sum to 81 (Brady et al. 2002: 14 and 15; Salloum et al. 2005: 27 and 25).
reporting_issues.consequence: The article does not say which count is randomized and which analysed; either way the valproic acid result rests on two small trials, one in people with bipolar disorder.

reporting_issues.issue: Table 1 footnote b explains an RD of −0.09 as 9% fewer participants returning to any drinking and a WMD of −8.8 as 8.8% fewer drinking days; both are absolute differences in percentage points, not relative reductions.
reporting_issues.consequence: Claims must state these as percentage points. Against a crude placebo return-to-any-drinking proportion of 83% in the acamprosate trials (editors' arithmetic from Figure 2), 9 points is a relative reduction of roughly a tenth (approximate, mixing a pooled RD with a crude proportion).

reporting_issues.issue: Table 2 does not state the naltrexone dose in the head-to-head trials, although the placebo-controlled analyses keep oral 50 mg/day, oral 100 mg/day and injectable naltrexone apart. By the review's own classification in Figures 2 and 3, the largest head-to-head trial (COMBINE) contributes the arm classed as 100 mg/day and the other three trials their 50 mg/day arms, and Table 2's participant totals equal those arms' sums (editors' arithmetic).
reporting_issues.consequence: The head-to-head estimates compare acamprosate with a mixture of two naltrexone groups, dominated by the group that showed no significant effect on return to any or heavy drinking against placebo in Table 1; the no-difference result cannot be read as a direct comparison with the 50 mg/day group behind the abstract's naltrexone NNTs.
